title: Istiqlal and Sheikh Zayed
hookLine: great modern mosques in Jakarta and Abu Dhabi

lines: ABU DHABI: WHITE MARBLE, OPEN DOORS.
cards: Jakarta, Friday, noon. Motorbikes thread between buses, and in the middle of it all stands a vast white mosque with a broad dome and a single tall minaret. Its name is one word: Istiqlal.
Independence. Across the road rises a Catholic cathedral with tall, pointed spires.

Now cross an ocean to Abu Dhabi: a mosque of white marble, domes like clustered pearls, flowers of colored stone set into the floors, and tour groups of every faith walking through in the late afternoon.
Two mosques, both raised in living memory. Today: Istiqlal and Sheikh Zayed.

teach.b: First, the name. Istiqlal is the Arabic word for independence, and the mosque was planned as the national mosque of a newly independent Indonesia.
A country that had just won its freedom chose to say so with a house of prayer. Second, the architect. The chosen design came from Friedrich Silaban, an Indonesian architect who was a Christian.
A Christian drew the plans for the national mosque, and it stands across from the cathedral. Some Indonesians point to that pair as a picture of neighbors living side by side. Third, Abu Dhabi.

teach.h: SHEIKH ZAYED: DOORS OPEN TO ALL.
teach.b: The Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque carries the name of the leader who founded the United Arab Emirates, and he is buried beside it.
Its builders gathered marble, stone, glass and craftsmen from many countries, and its doors stay open to visitors of every faith, with guides to explain what they're seeing.
Fourth, why build at all, when the whole earth is already a place of prayer?

teach.h: A HOUSE BUILT, A HOUSE IN PARADISE.
teach.b: A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says that whoever builds a mosque, seeking the face of God, God builds for him a house like it in Paradise. And the Qur'an says who keeps a mosque alive.

teach.h: HE ONLY SHALL TEND ALLAH'S SANCTUARIES.
teach.b: In Pickthall's translation: "He only shall tend Allah's sanctuaries who believeth in Allah and the Last Day." Marble and domes are one thing. Tending is another: the people who pray, sweep and teach there.
The Ka'ba, Medina, Jerusalem, Djenné, Jakarta, Abu Dhabi: every one of them was once new, once built today.

how: Large modern mosques often host Friday prayer, Ramadan night prayers and Eid gatherings, and some, like Sheikh Zayed in Abu Dhabi, welcome visitors with guided tours.

no one; the old mosque is simply enlarged.

practice: Find a photo of Istiqlal or Sheikh Zayed, or picture one, and walk through it slowly: the gate, the courtyard, the light on the floor, the shoes left in rows, the place where the prayer rows begin.
Somebody laid that floor, and somebody cleans it tonight. If you pray, remember the builders and the sweepers; if not, simply thank them in your mind.

wordCard.voice: Istiqlal, Indonesia's word for independence and the name its people gave the national mosque a Christian architect designed in Jakarta. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: independence, the name Indonesia gave its national mosque.

carryVoice: Your line: built today. Every old mosque, Mecca's included, was new once. See you tomorrow.
